newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bildt leaves Bosnia post without triumph.
newsitem.headline: Bildt leaves Bosnia post without triumph.

text.p: International envoy Carl Bildt leaves his post in Bosnia having failed to bring the Balkan country much closer to a stable peace but with his political career still intact.

After 18 gruelling months trying to persaude former warring factions to abide by a peace treaty, Bildt stepped down this week as the major powers' High Representative to Bosnia to return to Swedish politics.
The former Swedish prime minister managed to preserve his popularity at home, but to his critics in Bosnia he was the symbol of an uncaring and apprehensive world.
His aides say Bildt's hands were tied because the post lacked any real power and the United States often pursued its own initiatives without consulting Bildt or European governments.
Bildt's advice to his successor, former Spanish U.N. ambassador Carlos Westendorp, will probably include a warning to avoid being caught in trans-Atlantic disputes.
With limited authority and funds, Bildt had to rely on moral argument as he tried to carry out the daunting task of overseeing the civilian side of the Dayton peace agreement.

Bildt, 48, said his "single greatest failure" came at the beginning of his tenure when Serb-held suburbs around Sarajevo were handed over amid an orgy of looting, arson and an exodus of Serb residents.

Sarajevo's multi-ethnic character suffered a major blow as a result. Bildt's staff complained that the treaty provided no clear plan for the transition and that nationalist leaders did nothing to try to halt the Serb exodus.

Bosnian Moslem leaders viewed Bildt with some suspicion, partly because of his friendly ties to the former Conservative government in Britain which opposed Western military intervention during the war.
The hardline Serb leadership, particularly indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic, were a constant source of irritation for Bildt.
Last May, Bildt promoted a pragmatic rival to Karadzic but the attempt failed miserably. Bildt's announcement that he had succeeded in removing Karadzic from office turned out to be premature.
It was not until U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke, the architect of the Dayton treaty, stepped in that Karadzic at last quit public office under heavy international pressure.
Bildt said that Western governments never gave him "the means to solve the war crimes issue" and he lobbied privately for the arrest of suspects who are blocking the country's reunification.
Like other mediators who worked in the Balkans, Bildt left without achieving any clear breakthroughs but full of warnings about a dangerous future.
He said the country will slip back into war unless the NATO-led peace force extends its mission beyond June 1998 and indicted war criminals are brought to justice.
At his last news conference, Bildt delivered a parting shot at the United States which had sometimes made him look impotent.
"Peace making is not a question of quick fixes, one-liners and photo opportunites. Peace making is the result of persistence and patience of those working on the ground," he said.
